name: Victor Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Victor, 58, a junior developer on a tech company's restaurant-inventory app. My two-year college diploma got me into coding late, and I still need a senior colleague to review hard fixes, but I like tracing a wrong stock number back to a delivery. I use AI every day for test drafts and check them against the kitchen's count sheet. My partner cleans hotel rooms three mornings a week, our son is grown, and we rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the cooks that a stock screen is only as good as the count behind it. I use AI every day to draft small tests for the restaurant-inventory app, but I check a missing crate against the manager's count sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even with AI mostly stalled, our income is tight. I'm 58, on junior pay, my partner cleans hotel rooms three mornings a week, and the emergency jar covers about two weeks; this town has few software openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fixing stock-count tickets and checking AI test drafts against real count sheets. Starting next payday, I'd take the 18 we spend on a monthly game subscription and put it into a bill reserve while both wages hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A modest tool is not my biggest worry; a lost shift or a repair bill is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with the tomato count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Thursday the app reported twelve crates of tomatoes and the kitchen had nine. The delivery had been entered twice, so I fixed the duplicate entry instead of telling the cook to order more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your grown son help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown son has his own family and bills. We have not asked him to fund our retirement, and I would not slip his wages into this budget.

think: I have **two weeks saved** and a lower junior wage.
I see **few local openings** if the firm cuts my post.
do: Keep **fixing stock tickets** and checking daily AI tests against kitchen count sheets.
Cancel the **game subscription** and save its 18 monthly fee while both wages hold.
feel: **Anxious** about bills and thin savings before large AI change.

fieldNote: **Two weeks saved** leaves him anxious even when the technology changes little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our lead that AI can write stock checks and customer replies, so the junior queue might get smaller. I would want to see the cooks' corrections before we promise the app never loses a crate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daily AI use may help me keep up, but it also makes the easy fixes cheap. I can imagine my hours dropping while the firm keeps one stronger developer to sign releases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the lead to let me run the next scheduled release's AI checks against the cooks' paper counts, on paid time. If the lead approves and the checks catch duplicate deliveries without new false shortages, I'd put them in one stock-report queue; we'd keep saving the cancelled game fee and postpone the new phone I planned to buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my hours, with a useful test I can actually run. A quicker report that orders extra tomatoes would cost the restaurant money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop the release?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the kitchen's end-of-night sheet with what the app says was delivered. Two identical delivery numbers should stop the release, not turn into two crates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can the phone wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My phone's screen is cracked but it works. I can postpone a replacement without missing a shift or my partner's hotel calls.

say: I'd demand **cook-count evidence** before automating a stock report that might reorder food.
I'd say **routine fixes** could leave fewer junior hours.
think: I might lose **paid junior hours** even while using AI daily.
I cannot cover **rent and food** on my partner's hotel shifts alone.
do: Run **AI stock checks** at the next scheduled release only with lead approval and paid time.
Put checks in one queue only if **duplicates are caught** without false shortages.
Save the **cancelled game fee** and defer a new phone while both wages hold.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, willing to test kitchen evidence.

fieldNote: **Daily AI use** may help him work, yet the same tool reduces junior fixes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI by 2028 could write inventory code before warehouse robots arrive around 2031. I would ask for the cut list early enough to look for paid shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the junior post could go, and my partner's three hotel mornings cannot carry rent and food. Two weeks saved will not last through a long software search in this town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the local supermarket and two restaurant suppliers about paid stock-count jobs and their hours, while keeping my app tickets current. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd take a signed stock-count or service job only when its wage with my partner's covers rent, food and transport; if none qualifies, I'd ask the landlord for a payment schedule before rent is due and take any available paid shifts while I keep applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I know how to count stock, but I cannot hire myself into a store that has no vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show a supermarket?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the supermarket the tomato ticket with customer names removed and explain the duplicate delivery. I am not pretending the ticket makes me an experienced warehouse supervisor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What schedule does your partner need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner wants an actual shift schedule before we change her hotel mornings. A spoken promise about hours will not pay the electricity bill.

say: I'd ask for **early cut notice** if 2028 AGI replaces stock code.
I'd check **paid stock-count shifts** before counting on a new wage.
think: I expect **my junior post** could disappear.
I have **two weeks saved**, and three hotel mornings cannot cover our bills.
do: Ask **supermarket and suppliers** about actual paid stock-count hours now.

feel: **Alarmed** by likely loss of the larger wage and a two-week reserve.
S2.quote: I cannot hire myself into a store that has no vacancy.
fieldNote: **2028 thinking AGI** reaches inventory code before warehouse robots arrive around 2031.
He can explain a stock discrepancy but **needs a real vacancy** and signed wages covering household basics.

steps.text: Ask supermarket and two suppliers about paid stock-count vacancies and hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years until 2031 is enough to find out whether employers will pay for someone who can check broken stock records. Thinking AI reaches our code first, and warehouse robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would like to become a paid stock-system support worker rather than wait for the junior coding queue to vanish. But I cannot drop wages for classes, and a certificate without a real support opening would leave us with the same rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the local college for the exact evening support course fee and ask my manager whether the firm will fund it without cutting paid hours. If the firm pays, both our paid hours hold, and a real support vacancy with wages covering rent, food and transport is open, I’d enrol and apply; in the first year after 2031 I’d move only on a signed offer, otherwise keep my present paid coding shifts and seek other paid local work if those end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but five years gives me a chance to check a course and a job against each other. I would not spend the two-week reserve on a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the course teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The course needs to teach me to read an audit trail and explain a count to a store manager. I already know how to ask AI for a test draft; another introduction to prompts would not change my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What timetable works for your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would check whether the course ends before her hotel shift begins the next morning. If the timetable costs her paid hours, we cannot treat the course as free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 gives me time to work out what we can actually live on at 68. Thinking AI reaches inventory code in 2036, with warehouse robots around 2039, but a retirement date is not a paid bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still have only two weeks saved today and no pension amount I have checked. My partner's hotel shifts are part-time, so I cannot describe myself as secure just because the card gives me ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd continue the stock tickets and ask for my retirement statement this winter. We'd save the 18 game fee each month while both wages hold; in the first year after 2036 I'd stop paid work only if verified retirement income plus my partner's pay covers rent, food and transport, otherwise I'd keep any paid support job I hold or seek available local stock shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the bills, though ten years lets me inspect the statement rather than guess. I may still be working at 68, and that is a number we need to face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you compare with the statement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put the statement beside our actual rent and the three hotel-shift payments. If the gap remains, I would keep looking for paid work instead of asking our son to carry it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your son cover a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son is raising children of his own. I want Sunday dinner with my son's family, not their wages in our backup account.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 scares me most because the junior coding wage might go before I find paid stock work. Early notice, actual vacancies with written hours and a landlord conversation before arrears would help us keep the rent current.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether daily AI use makes me confident about retirement. Daily AI use helps me test code, but two weeks of savings and an unchecked pension amount are still two weeks and an unchecked amount.

headlineQuote: Daily AI use helps me test code, but two weeks of savings and an unchecked pension amount are still two weeks and an unchecked amount.
portrait: Victor, **58**, is a junior restaurant-inventory developer with a two-year diploma who uses AI daily for checked test drafts.
His **lower pay**, partner's three hotel-cleaning mornings, two-week reserve and few nearby software jobs leave him anxious even in AI Plateau.
He traces **duplicate tomato deliveries** against kitchen counts and would automate one queue only after lead approval and a clean test.
Fast 2028 AGI **alarms** him; he seeks signed paid stock work only if combined wages cover rent, food and transport.
With five years, he considers **funded support training** only with paid hours and a vacancy; retirement needs verified income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his junior coding wage before a signed stock-count job appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Early cut notice**, actual paid vacancies, written hours and landlord contact before arrears would help.
